Curious when the "year of our lord" started and how history was recorded before that.
When did societies begin using the current calendar system for what year it is(2015 a.d.) What year was it before then and what did they base it off?

I know that the Julian calendar came before the Georgian and that the Georgian was introduced by one of the Popes names George to move the date of Easter.

Here is a wiki on Julian calendar https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_calendar and on the Gregorian calendar https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar

"Gregorian" and Pope Gregory.

Check the calendar for September 1752 (Apple's calendar apps get it wrong) for when the UK changed the calendar to adopt the Gregorian system. Different countries made the change at different times, with Russia not changing until 1912.

http://i.imgur.com/GxPN302.png

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorian_calendar

Also, why is October (octo=8) the tenth month?
because march was the first month of the year.
Which is why leap day is at the end of February - it used to be at the end of the year under the old Roman system.

I'm not a calendar expert by any means, but if you're tasked with making a new calender system, you probably need a historical date to be your arbitrary starting point. I believe it started as an issue of trying to forget the system used by the men who persecuted Christians. Then we had the Julian Calender system that sought to correct the Roman calendar system. Now we finally have the Gregorian calendar system which corrected the Julian Calendar by a percentage of like .02% or something like that.

So I have really gotten a bunch of links. Let me see if I can piece together an answer from those as it is not really answered in a straight-forward manner.

  • First to note that not all societies use the current Gregorian Calendar systems. (such as: Saudi Arabia, which uses the Islamic calendar for all purposes, Ethiopia, Ethiopian calendar, and Iran and Afghanistan) - thanks /u/ginx for bringing that up

  • Most Western countries adopted the Gregorian between late 1500 (such as Venice in 1582) and late 1700 (such as UK in 1752).

  • October used to be the eight month due to Romans starting the year when politicians would enter office (thanks users /u/wullie and /u/schroedingers-fuck):

probably 1 May before 222 BC, 15 March from 222 BC and 1 January from 153 BC. - wikipedia

  • No easy way to answer what year they used before that as at this point the change came from Julian to Gregorian, thus the years and months were very similar and often off by only a little:

it was often necessary to indicate the date of some event in both the Julian calendar and in the Gregorian calendar, for example, "10/21 February 1750/51", where the dual year accounts for some countries already beginning their numbered year on 1 January while others were still using some other date. Even before 1582, the year sometimes had to be double dated because of the different beginnings of the year in various countries. Woolley, writing in his biography of John Dee (1527–1608/9), notes that immediately after 1582 English letter writers "customarily" used "two dates" on their letters, one OS and one NS. - wikipedia

  • Before the current Anno Domini dating was the Roman Calendar (AUC), which began its year dating with the founding of Rome, roughly 753 BC thus making 1 AD = 754 AUC. The Anno Domini calendar year dating was proposed by a monk in 525 AD or 1279 AUC. Therefore I guess I would say that it was the year 1279 when modern civilization adopted the AD into 525 AD. The year is what was changed as the Roman Calendar was already on the Julian calendar which is very similar to the Gregorian we use today.

The Anno Domini year numbering was developed by a monk named Dionysius Exiguus in Rome during 525 - wikipedia

tl;dr - Roman calendar AUC would have been at 1279 when the Julian calendar was created with dating of AD in what is today 525 AD. Short answer, 1279 AUC to 525 AD. If still on AUC it would currently be the year 2768 AUC.
